section_title: What will Gog’s defeat make known?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 “As for you, O son of man, prophesy against Gog and declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. 2 I will turn you around, drive you along, bring you up from the far north, and send you against the mountains of Israel. 3 Then I will strike the bow from your left hand and dash down the arrows from your right hand. 4 On the mountains of Israel you will fall—you and all your troops and the nations with you. I will give you as food to every kind of ravenous bird and wild beast. 5 You will fall in the open field, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.

6 I will send fire on Magog and on those who dwell securely in the coastlands, and they will know that I am the LORD. 7 So I will make My holy name known among My people Israel and will no longer allow it to be profaned. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, the Holy One in Israel. 8 Yes, it is coming, and it will surely happen, declares the Lord GOD. This is the day of which I have spoken.

context_lines: The prophecy returns to Gog’s defeat and begins to describe its aftermath. The Lord brings the invader against Israel’s mountains, strikes the bow and arrows from his hands, and declares that he and his forces will fall.

The army that came to take the land will become food for birds and wild animals. Fire will also reach Magog and those dwelling securely in the coastlands. The judgment is not confined to the soldiers’ immediate position.

The Lord’s holy name is central. He will make it known among His people and before the nations, and will no longer allow it to be profaned. The closing assurance treats His promise as certain: the day He has spoken of will come.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/39.htm) understands the destruction as a miraculous act by which the Lord makes His name known. [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/39.htm) treats the disabled bow as a picture of the failure of the invaders’ weapons generally.
The emphasis is the same: the army’s equipment cannot preserve it when the Lord acts against it. His people’s security rests on His faithfulness.
